Area.evidence_source: The negative impact of the participants' adverse relationship with their families seems to have undermined their coping and help-seeking behavior, as evidenced in their unstable relationships with peers and significant others, and in some cases, constricted perceptions of circumstances in times of interpersonal conflicts and distress.Ten of the 12 interviewees (83%) were characterized by their family members or mental health providers as reticent and keeping their worries to themselves. Nine of the interviewees (75%) made statements indicating that they felt "no one can help" during times of distress. Implicit in their remarks was a lack of trust in themselves and others, resulting in difficulties in reaching out for support in times of distress for fear of rejection and criticism.A middle-aged male participant reflected on his isolation from family and peers: "There is no one who understands my feelings. I have hidden my problems from others. As a result, I have never asked for help, and I do feel very lonely."A young female participant described her interpersonal stress on the job: "Every time I start a job, if people don't talk to me, I will not talk to them either. And then I would blame myself thinking that it's because I am not attractive or too fat."A young female participant talked about how her parents tended to get upset with her and criticize her when she was growing up: "I guess I bottled up my emotions. Even now I am never too keen on talking, especially about difficult subjects."A female participant talked about why she decided not to call her young son in her home country since she sent him away a couple of years ago: "I am not a chatty person. If I dwell on my stress I will feel sad. So I often told myself not to think about my son and other worries."
